Schools and movements

Cross-cultural psychology

Checking whether what we know holds across cultures.

What does it propose?Many conclusions in psychology are based on a specific kind of person. We need to check which are universal and which depend on culture.
What does it study?Differences and similarities between cultures in perception, emotion, personality, values, development and mental health.
How does it study it?Comparative studies with samples from many countries, careful translation and adaptation of instruments, and collaboration with local researchers.
Who took part?Harry Triandis, Geert Hofstede, Shalom Schwartz, Richard Nisbett, Hazel Markus and Shinobu Kitayama; Joseph Henrich, Steven Heine and Ara Norenzayan (WEIRD).
What remains?Awareness that most participants came from Western societies, and the effort to diversify samples.
What is debated?Categories such as 'individualism' and 'collectivism' are big simplifications, and differences within a country can be larger than between countries.

Context

As early as 1898, the Cambridge expedition to the Torres Strait measured the perception of the islanders, and in the 1930s Alexander Luria studied the reasoning of peasants in Uzbekistan. But cross-cultural psychology as an organised field was born in the 1960s and 1970s, with the founding of the Journal of Cross-Cultural Psychology (1970).

Well-known findings

  • The Müller-Lyer illusion affects some hunter-gatherer populations much less, according to the study by Segall, Campbell and Herskovits (1966).
  • Hazel Markus and Shinobu Kitayama (1991) described an "independent self", more common in Western societies, versus an "interdependent self", more common in East Asia.
  • Richard Nisbett found differences in attention: East Asian participants paid more attention to the context of a scene and Americans more to the main object.
  • Some emotional expressions are fairly well recognised across cultures, although the rules on when to show them vary widely.

The WEIRD problem

In 2010 Joseph Henrich, Steven Heine and Ara Norenzayan showed that most psychology participants came from Western, educated, industrialised, rich and democratic (WEIRD) societies, a group unrepresentative of humanity. Since then studies with samples from many countries have multiplied, though the imbalance remains large.

Cultural dimensions

In the 1970s Geert Hofstede analysed surveys of IBM employees in dozens of countries and proposed dimensions such as individualism-collectivism, power distance and uncertainty avoidance. Shalom Schwartz studied values in over 60 countries and found a structure of ten basic values that appears in almost all of them, although their relative importance varies.

Adapting treatments

Psychological therapies can be adapted to the culture of those receiving them: language, examples, the role of the family or beliefs about distress. Meta-analyses suggest that culturally adapted interventions work somewhat better than non-adapted ones with cultural minorities.

A school's historical importance and the current scientific support for its ideas are different things: we explain them separately.
